t.2.2.2: With a mighty voice like the sound of a kettledrum, deep and resonant, the king, making the hall resound like a thundercloud, spoke.
t.2.2.3: I, then, wish to unite with welfare this entire world, which deserves happiness and was protected by the former Ikṣvāku kings.
t.2.2.4: I too have followed the path trodden by my forebears, ever tireless, guarding my subjects to the best of my power.
t.2.2.5: Pursuing the welfare of the whole world, I have worn out this body, now grown pale, in the shade of this royal parasol.
t.2.2.7: For I am wearied from bearing the heavy yoke of the world's dharma, a burden attended by royal might and hard to carry for those who have not conquered their senses.
t.2.2.6: Having lived for many thousands of years and passed through many lifespans, I now long for rest for this worn-out body.
t.2.2.8: Therefore I wish to rest, having appointed my son to the welfare of the people, after gaining the consent of all these foremost of the twice-born gathered here near me.
t.2.2.9: For my eldest son Rāma, conqueror of enemy cities and equal to Puraṃdara in valor, takes after me in all virtues.
t.2.2.10: Gladly shall I unite him, the best of those who uphold dharma, that bull among men, with the office of crown prince, as the moon is united with Puṣya.
t.2.2.11: That glorious elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa is a lord worthy of you; with him as lord, even the three worlds would be better protected.
t.2.2.12: By uniting this earth at once with this blessing and entrusting it to that son of mine, I shall surely be freed from my burden of care.
t.2.2.13: As the king spoke thus, the delighted kings joyfully applauded him, as peacocks hail a great rain-bearing cloud as it thunders.
t.2.2.14: Having fully grasped the intention of him who knew dharma and artha, and having understood in their minds that King Daśaratha was old, they spoke.
t.2.2.15: You are old, O king, having lived many thousands of years; therefore consecrate Rāma, that prince, as heir apparent.
t.2.2.16: Having heard their words, which were pleasing to his heart, the king, as if he did not know and wishing to find out, spoke these words.
t.2.2.17: How is it that, while I am ruling the earth in accordance with dharma, you sirs wish to see my son as crown prince?
t.2.2.18: Together with the townspeople and the country folk, they said to that great-souled one: "O king, your son has many auspicious virtues."
t.2.2.20: Rāma is a true and good man in the world, wholly devoted to truth and righteousness; he knows dharma, is true to his word, is virtuous in conduct, and is free from envy.
t.2.2.19: In divine qualities Rāma, whose valor is true, is equal to Śakra; indeed, O lord of the people, he surpasses even all the Ikṣvākus.
t.2.2.21: He is forbearing, a giver of comfort, gentle of speech, grateful, and master of his senses; mild and steadfast of mind, he is ever auspicious and free from envy.
t.2.2.22: Rāghava speaks kindly to all beings and speaks the truth, and he is one who honors and attends upon learned, aged brāhmaṇas.
t.2.2.24: Whenever he goes to battle for the sake of a village or a city, having gone there accompanied by Saumitri, he does not return without having conquered.
t.2.2.23: Because of this, his incomparable renown, glory and splendour grow here in this world. He is skilled in all the weapons of the gods, the Asuras and men.
t.2.2.25: Returning from battle on an elephant or a chariot, he always asks the citizens about their welfare, as though they were his own kin.
t.2.2.26: About their sons, their sacred fires, their wives, and their bands of servants and disciples, he inquires fully and in proper order, as a father would about his own true-born sons.
t.2.2.28: In the misfortunes of the people he becomes deeply grieved, and in all their festivities he rejoices like a father.
t.2.2.27: “Do your disciples serve you, and are they girded and ready for their tasks?” In this way Rāma, a tiger among men, always speaks to us.
t.2.2.29: Truthful in speech, a mighty archer, devoted to the service of elders, with his senses subdued, your dear son Rāghava has, by good fortune, been born to bring you the highest welfare. By good fortune he is endowed with the virtues of a son, like Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
t.2.2.30: All the people, in the kingdom and likewise in the capital city, wish for strength, health and long life for Rāma, whose self is well known.
t.2.2.31: The people both inside and outside the city, the townsfolk and the country folk, and the women, old and young alike, morning and evening, with minds intent and composed…
t.2.2.32: They bow down to all the gods for the sake of the illustrious Rāma; O lord, may their prayer be fulfilled through your grace.
t.2.2.33: We would see Rāma, dark as the blue lotus, the slayer of all his enemies, your son, the son of the foremost of kings, established in the position of heir apparent.
t.2.2.34: O granter of boons, for our welfare you should quickly and joyfully consecrate that son of yours, who is like the god of gods, devoted to the good of all the world, and cherished by the noble.
